Action: reproduce their probe (loopback server that sends Accept-CH, visit twice) against a cuttle seed and compare Sec-CH-DPR / Sec-CH-Device-Memory / Sec-CH-Viewport-Width against the JS values; then plumb both through one function rather than stripping hints.

items.what: Open question with no maintainer answer yet: 'Could you please explain why navigator.deviceMemory is capped at 8 with the comment "real Chrome never reports >8"?' Reporter is on Chrome 151.0.7922.138 and shows a screenshot of stock Chrome reporting the real value on a 32 GB machine. Issue #11's control run independently confirms it: stock Chrome 150 reports 32 on a 32 GB host in BOTH the JS channel and the Sec-CH-Device-Memory header, which contradicts the Device Memory API spec (spec says quantize and cap at 8) - shipping Chrome no longer honours the cap.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: ~/Projects/cuttle/internal/fingerprint/args.go lines 260-273 hardcodes `--fingerprint-device-memory=8` for every Apple Silicon entry, with a comment asserting as fact: 'Chrome clamps navigator.deviceMemory to a maximum of 8 ... so 8 is the only value a real Mac can report.' Two independent reports on current Chrome say that clamp is gone. If true, every cuttle macOS persona reports 8 GB on a machine whose GPU string claims an M3 Max - and a stock-Chrome comparison is a one-line detection. This is a golden.json regeneration plus a comment rewrite; the only work is verifying against a real Chrome 151 first.

items.what: Community reported clearcote felt sluggish vs plain ungoogled-chromium, with a video of a DOM loop benchmark. Root cause was not the stealth patches at all: 'The published binary was compiled without the optimisations a normal Chrome release is built with, and with a large set of internal development-time checks left switched on.' Rebuild medians: DOM create-20k-elements+layout 1514ms -> 133ms, DOM query+style read 101ms -> 11ms, Date.now() 120ns -> 40ns; binary 406 MB -> 278 MB. The diagnostic that makes it conclusive is the two CONTROLS: pure-JS loops (JIT math 45.0 -> 45.8ms, typed-array 6.0 -> 5.8ms) barely move because V8 generates that code at runtime, so anything that regresses must be crossing into C++ (DOM, layout, bindings). Fix is live only in their Pro 151 line; the public 149 build still ships the slow binary and the issue is deliberately left open until a rebuilt free binary lands.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: cuttle self-builds its Chromium in packages/browser/build with its own GN args, so it can fall into the identical trap (is_debug, dcheck_always_on, is_official_build, symbol_level, thin LTO/PGO). Two consequences: agent runs get slower for free, and — more importantly for a stealth product — timing IS a fingerprint surface; a browser whose DOM operations are 10x slower than any real Chrome is measurable from the page in a few milliseconds, on top of cuttle's already-costly humanization (~0.5s/click, ~130ms/char). Cheapest possible check: run their control-vs-DOM benchmark pair inside the container and compare against stock Chrome; then audit the GN args. Their control-loop trick is also worth stealing outright as a permanent check in packages/browser/validate/.

items.what: With a spoofed WebRTC IP set, TURN Allocate requests go out over UDP straight from the host interface, outside the proxy - six retransmissions from one source port, observed by a listener bound to the host's LAN address (not loopback). Diagnosis, confirmed by the maintainer: --webrtc-ip-handling-policy=disable_non_proxied_udp is applied during candidate GATHERING, and TURN allocation is not gathering, so a page naming its own turn:...?transport=udp server walks straight past a check that does catch STUN. The page-visible ICE surface shows only the spoofed address, so nothing in the page indicates a leak - only the TURN operator (i.e. the fingerprinter) sees it. Second finding in the same thread: the spoofed srflx candidates are FABRICATED, not measured - pointing at an unroutable STUN address (192.0.2.1) returns the same 4 candidates at the same latency, and '4 srflx candidates above 0 host candidates' is self-contradicting (a reflexive candidate is by definition a host candidate seen from outside) and trivially detectable from the page. Third finding, the sharpest one: setting the WebRTC address RELAXES UDP suppression that was otherwise holding - with the option unset, the same request produces zero datagrams. Fixed in their Pro engine; the fixed shape is 1 srflx + 2 mDNS-concealed host candidates, 0 datagrams escaping.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: cuttle sets a WebRTC exit IP per seed in internal/fingerprint/ and relies on Chromium's WebRTC IP handling policy for the rest. Both halves apply: run their rig (UDP listener on the host's LAN address, page names its own turn:...?transport=udp) against a cuttle seed behind a proxy, and separately count srflx-vs-host candidates from the page. If cuttle emits reflexive candidates with no host candidates, that is a zero-baseline detection sitting in the default configuration - and it would not show up anywhere in golden.json, because the golden only snapshots the args, not the resulting ICE shape.

items.what: Feature request, shipped: profile cookies were the one part of a user-data-dir that could not be copied between machines, because the cookie key is wrapped by DPAPI/Keychain. The reporter's critique of the obvious workaround is the transferable part: reading context.cookies() on a timer is 'a poll rather than a store' and has four structural failures - it must run forever for every live profile; everything since the last poll is lost; the ORDINARY exit path (user closes the last window, or a crash, or a kill) cannot be saved at all because the API needs a live browser; and session cookies need the export most while being least likely to survive it. Maintainer took the profile-held-key option and shipped it in PRO r14 / SDK 0.26.0 as `portableProfile: true` or a caller-supplied `encryptionKey`. Two design facts worth keeping: Chromium registers cookie key providers with a PRECEDENCE where only the highest encrypts but EVERY registered provider can still decrypt, so adding a portable provider above the platform ones migrates existing profiles automatically with no export/import step and no new format; and on Linux this already works today with `--password-store=basic`, because the POSIX key provider derives from a hardcoded constant. Stated plainly rather than buried: a key stored next to the data it protects means the cookie DB is effectively unencrypted at rest, hence opt-in and off by default.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: cuttle's per-seed auth-state snapshot/restore in internal/serve/ (cookies + per-origin localStorage over CDP) IS the poll-not-store pattern the reporter dismantles - it shares every one of the four failure modes, including the one that matters most in practice: a container stop or an OOM kill loses whatever happened since the last snapshot, and session cookies never survive. Since cuttle's container is Linux, the maintainer's Linux note is the immediate win: adding `--password-store=basic` to the launch args makes the whole seed profile dir copyable as-is, so `cuttle purge-profile`'s inverse (export/import a warm logged-in seed, or persist it to a volume) becomes a directory copy instead of a CDP dance. That could let the snapshot/restore code be deleted rather than generalized.

items.what: Canvas readback noise was applied unconditionally, so a single fillRect() in one flat colour read back as EIGHT distinct colours (22 of 4096 pixels perturbed by +1 on some combination of R/G/B; alpha never touched; 8 = the 2^3 channel combinations). Detection is five lines of JS with no reference device, no fingerprint corpus and no cross-session correlation - a boolean computed locally in milliseconds. The reporter's framing is the reusable insight: 'a site that can cheaply determine THAT noise is present does not need the identifier - the presence of instrumentation is itself the classification. A browser reporting a mainstream Windows GPU, a stock user agent and a coherent client-hint set, which also fails a flat-fill test, has told the site MORE than an unprotected canvas would have.' Fix: gate the readback perturbation on a uniformity predicate that exits on the first differing pixel, so flat regions are returned untouched and varying content pays only a handful of comparisons. Reasoning recorded alongside: a flat region is byte-identical on every machine, so there was never a per-machine signal there to conceal - skipping it costs zero unlinkability. The verification deliberately checks BOTH directions, because '0 pixels differ' would be equally true if noise had simply been switched off.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: cuttle ships no canvas-noise patch (there is no canvas patch in packages/browser/patches - clark's canvas noise is not in our 24-patch series), so the literal bug does not apply. But packages/browser/patches/0026-audio-fingerprint-noise.patch is the same mechanism on a different surface, and the analogous defect is exactly as cheap to detect: if the audio noise perturbs a constant or silent buffer, an AudioContext rendering a DC-offset or silence comes back non-constant, which no real browser produces. Worth adding both the uniformity-predicate idea and, more importantly, the BOTH-DIRECTIONS test (noise absent on flat input AND still present on varying input) to packages/browser/validate/.

items.what: A WebGL2 context advertised the WebGL1 extension list, so 16 advertised extensions returned null from getExtension() - every one of them a WebGL1 name that WebGL2 absorbed into core (ANGLE_instanced_arrays, OES_vertex_array_object, WEBGL_depth_texture, WEBGL_draw_buffers, ...), which is the signature of the wrong list. Detection needs no baseline, just two calls: getSupportedExtensions().filter(n => gl.getExtension(n) === null). 'Advertising an extension and then refusing to hand it over is not something a real driver does.' The fix generalizes better than the bug: the advertised set and the objects backing it are now enforced to agree in BOTH directions - nothing advertised may fail to resolve, and nothing a profile omits may remain quietly functional - with WEBGL_debug_renderer_info the one deliberate exception since it carries identity strings but no capability. An empty per-version list falls through to the real set rather than borrowing the other version's, so a partial profile cannot produce a hybrid no driver ships. The same thread carries a subtler lesson the maintainer nearly got wrong: four stencil masks are MUTABLE GL state, so applying captured values the way immutable capabilities are applied would produce gl.stencilMask(0x12) followed by getParameter(STENCIL_WRITEMASK) returning the capture's value - a set-then-read contradiction detectable with no reference data at all, strictly worse than the mismatch it fixes. Captured masks are now served only until the context writes stencil state.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: cuttle spoofs WebGL identity in packages/browser/patches/0016-webgl-vendor-renderer-from-cli.patch and WebGPU in 0049-webgpu-adapter-info-coherent.patch. The immutable-vs-mutable distinction is the part to internalize: any spoofed value that page JS can also WRITE must fall back to the real value after a write, or it becomes a set-then-read self-contradiction. Worth auditing 0049 and 0016 for the same hazard, and worth adding an advertised-vs-resolvable reconciliation check (both directions) to packages/browser/validate/ - this is the class of bug golden.json structurally cannot catch, because the golden snapshots the ARGS, not what the running engine actually reports.

items.what: Buried at the end of the maintainer's #11 reply, flagged as a real defect being tracked separately: 'Persona screen dimensions with real pointer coordinates and inconsistently overridden window.screenX/outerWidth is the same shape of defect, and "window measures wider than the screen it reports being on" is exactly the kind of self-contradiction that needs no baseline to detect.' Reinforced in #17 by a design constraint the maintainer states before writing any code: window.outerHeight - window.innerHeight is the browser chrome height and is readable by any page, so a profile-label UI must live INSIDE the existing toolbar height, never as an extra row - the acceptance test is that outerHeight - innerHeight must be byte-identical to a stock build with the flag and without it. 'That would be a self-inflicted signal, and a worse trade than the usability problem it solves.'
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: This is cuttle's known pain #1 stated as a stealth bug rather than a cosmetic one. internal/fingerprint/args.go sizes --window-size to the seed's SPOOFED screen table inside a fixed 1920x1080 Xvfb framebuffer, and packages/browser/patches/0011-screen-dimensions-from-cli.patch + 0013-window-outer-and-dpr.patch override screen and outerWidth/Height - but MouseEvent.screenX/screenY are derived by Blink from the real window position plus client coords, and internal/serve/humanize.go dispatches Input.dispatchMouseEvent without touching them. So the tempting fix for the viewer complaint (just make the window fill 1920x1080) would break the spoofed-screen coherence, and the current state may already leak via pointer coordinates. The right move is to make the framebuffer, the window size, the spoofed screen and the pointer coordinate space one coherent set per seed - which also solves the viewer-fill complaint properly instead of trading stealth for it.

items.what: Feature request to visually label a running profile inside the browser window, because several identical browsers on one desktop means 'telling them apart currently means clicking into a window and inferring which account it is from what happens to be on screen, which is slow and easy to get wrong - and getting it wrong means acting in the wrong account.' Maintainer's response adds three things: --window-name is upstream Chromium and only fixes the OUTSIDE (taskbar, alt-tab), not the focused window; Windows taskbar grouping is keyed on AppUserModelID which Chromium derives from the profile path, so separate user-data-dirs should already land in separate groups and the genuinely missing half is the per-profile ICON; and colour is the part that SCALES - 'text has to be read one window at a time; a tint is matched pre-attentively, so at a dozen windows the colour does most of the work', which is why label and labelColor should ship together rather than colour being a later addition. Deprioritized behind an intermittent stability issue: 'a profile label does not help much on a browser that occasionally goes down.'
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: cuttle is a multi-seed farm fronted by ONE KasmVNC viewer at :6080 showing one 1920x1080 desktop with openbox - the same 'which window is which account' problem, worse, because every seed's window is on the same screen with the same icon and the human is doing captcha handoff under time pressure. cuttle already knows each window's seed, so a per-seed openbox window title and a per-seed colour applied at the window-manager level (openbox titlebar/border theme, or a wmctrl-set title) gets the whole benefit with ZERO page-visible surface - no Chrome chrome is touched, so outerHeight - innerHeight is untouched by construction. That sidesteps the exact constraint that is blocking clearcote. Maps to ops/docker/bin/ and the per-seed pool in internal/serve/.

items.what: Reporter: loading fingerprint.com kills the renderer every attempt on Chrome 149, Playwright's crash event fires, the tab is unrecoverable, and evaluate() then throws 'Target crashed'; creepjs.org/checker dies the same way after ~35s, once it finishes collecting. Reproduces with NO fingerprint option, on a bare launchPersistentContext, no proxy, no capture. Maintainer could not reproduce on 151 and refused to claim it fixed - two explanations fit (a 149-era bug incidentally resolved by the version bump, or something environment-dependent in GPU/driver/memory) and he asked for chrome://gpu, whether it survives with --disable-gpu (which separates a GPU-process crash from a renderer one), and any Crashpad report. The volunteered part is the useful one: 'during unrelated testing on 151 we twice saw a browser die with a target-closed error - once after POINTER INPUT, once on a page that never finished loading - roughly two runs in a dozen.'
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: Two hooks. (1) 'A renderer crash on a fingerprinting page is very often GPU-process related' plus the --disable-gpu bisection is a diagnostic cuttle should keep, because the container renders via --use-angle=swiftshader under Xvfb, i.e. permanently on the software path that fingerprinting pages hammer hardest. (2) 'a browser died after pointer input, roughly two runs in a dozen' is worth watching against internal/serve/humanize.go, which synthesizes far more Input.dispatchMouseEvent traffic than a normal driver (Fitts-law curved paths with per-step tremor). cuttle's immortal keep-alive tab protects against a driver teardown killing Chrome, but not against the renderer itself dying mid-run - worth confirming the pool's launch-backoff path actually recovers a seed whose renderer crashed rather than whose browser exited.

items.what: Long feature thread on runtime TLS ClientHello / JA3 control (pointing at chromium-with-custom-tls-fingerprints). The maintainer's reply is the highest-signal design argument in the repo: clearcote already sends a GENUINE current-Chromium ClientHello including Chrome's per-connection extension-order randomization (default since Chrome 110), therefore 'a fixed JA3 is itself a signal - real Chrome does not have a stable JA3; it varies every connection. Pinning one value can look LESS like Chrome, not more.' (This is why JA4, order-insensitive, exists.) The higher-value goal is matching the TLS shape to the Chrome version the persona already CLAIMS - cipher list, version bounds, the post-quantum key-share that changed across recent Chrome majors - while keeping Chrome-like randomization. And TLS is only one layer: the HTTP/2 fingerprint (SETTINGS frame / pseudo-header order) and QUIC/H3 sit right next to it, so 'a signature that is coherent at TLS but not at H2 is still incoherent overall.' Requester converged on the same conclusion and asked for one stable-but-randomly-generated network persona per profile derived from the saved UA/browser-family/version/platform, with arbitrary JA3 kept as a documented escape hatch. Their own docs/RESEARCH.md (added via PR #6's neighbourhood) is blunter: building on Chromium 149 while spoofing an older UA leaks at TLS because 149 adds ML-DSA sigalgs 0x904-0x906, and 'a major anti-bot service flags UA 148 + TLS 149'.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: cuttle does no TLS work at all, and packages/browser/patches/0007-user-agent-client-hints-from-cli.patch lets a seed advertise an arbitrary Chrome brand/version while the binary is ungoogled-chromium 148 (versions.env). The moment a seed's claimed version diverges from 148, the UA-vs-TLS mismatch described above is live. The cheap, KISS-compatible action is NOT to build TLS spoofing - it is to constrain the client-hints arg-builder so a seed can never claim a Chrome major that the pinned build's ClientHello does not match, and to record that constraint in internal/fingerprint. The 'fixed JA3 is a tell' point also pre-empts anyone proposing a JA3 knob for cuttle.

items.what: Two 'please support mobile/iOS' requests consolidated, and refused with reasoning worth keeping. On Android: 'Android support in clearcote is a PERSONA, not a port. The browser is a desktop build presenting a coherent Android Chrome device ... That works because clearcote IS Chrome: Android Chrome and desktop Chrome are the same engine, so the values presented and the engine underneath agree. Nothing has to be faked below the surface.' On iOS: browsers there are WebKit (Chrome for iOS is a WKWebView wrapper), so there is no engine to modify and the fallback of injecting script is exactly what a check running in a Worker exposes; and presenting a Safari persona from Blink is refused because JavaScriptCore and V8 differ in error message text, stack trace format, Function.prototype.toString output, Intl and number formatting - 'a long tail of API surface, all readable in a line or two of script, none of it changed by a UA string ... We would rather not ship it than ship something convincing in the UA that falls apart on the first real check.' Also, from evaluating a linked Android fork, two ideas explicitly adopted: (1) COHERENCE VALIDATION AS A BUILD-TIME GATE - validate a generated device profile for internal consistency BEFORE it is ever used and fail loudly when two coupled fields disagree, run in CI over a large sample of generated identities, because that is a better place to catch the class than a browser test; (2) bind more of a persona to a SINGLE hardware identity rather than sampling traits independently.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: The build-time coherence gate is the concrete steal. cuttle's internal/fingerprint/testdata/golden.json is a REGRESSION tripwire - it proves the output did not change, not that the output is self-consistent - so a coherent-but-wrong combination (M3 Max GPU string with deviceMemory 8, or a spoofed screen smaller than the window) passes forever once golden. Adding a coherence property test in internal/fingerprint that sweeps many seeds and asserts cross-field invariants (screen >= window size, GPU family vs core count vs memory, persona platform vs UA vs timezone vs locale vs Apple-Silicon pinning) is small Go work with no new dependency and catches exactly what the golden cannot. The 'persona not port' framing is also the right answer to any future ask for a mobile or Safari persona on cuttle's Blink build.

items.what: PR adding docs/CANVAS-BRIDGE.md - forward canvas2D/WebGL OPERATIONS (geometry, shaders, uniforms, draws, procedural textures, readPixels, toDataURL, measureText) over a WebSocket to a remote real-GPU browser reached over CDP, and return that browser's authentic pixels; local farbling noise is bypassed on the bridge path because the bridged pixels are ground truth. Premise, stated flatly: 'you cannot make one GPU emit another GPU's exact pixels in software', so spoofing only the WebGL vendor/renderer STRING while rendering locally means strict checks that compare rendered pixels against the claimed hardware notice the mismatch. Operational rules that generalize: the render GPU IS your canvas identity, so pick a real CONSUMER GPU and explicitly AVOID a software rasterizer (SwiftShader / llvmpipe / 'Basic Render Driver') or a datacenter card - both are internally coherent but stick out as non-consumer hardware; and one render host = one canvas identity, so every profile sharing a render host is linkable by canvas hash. Step 4 of the tutorial insists you must ALSO pass --fingerprint-gpu-vendor/--fingerprint-gpu-renderer matching the render GPU, 'or the string and the pixels disagree'. Canvases sourcing textures from images/video/3D fall back to local rendering rather than returning half-rendered.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: This is the sharpest external challenge to a claim cuttle makes about itself. ops/docker/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh line 39 launches with --use-angle=swiftshader, while internal/fingerprint/args.go advertises ANGLE Metal 'Apple M1/M2/M3/M3 Max' or Windows D3D11 renderer strings - i.e. a software rasterizer rendering the pixels behind a discrete/integrated-GPU string. internal/cli/SKILL.md lines 464-468 tells agents this is fine ('a probe of the running seed returns a coherent spoofed GPU ... not SwiftShader'), which is true of the STRING and says nothing about the PIXELS. clearcote's whole bridge exists because that gap is scored by strict checks. cuttle should not build a canvas bridge (KISS/YAGNI, and it needs an external GPU host), but it should (a) measure the gap - hash a canvas/WebGL probe in the container vs on a real Mac/PC with the same claimed GPU, (b) soften the SKILL.md claim to be about strings specifically, and (c) treat 'a shared software rasterizer means every cuttle seed on a host shares one canvas hash and is cross-linkable' as a known limitation to document rather than discover.

items.what: docs/RESEARCH.md, the blueprint referenced from the canvas-bridge PR, synthesized from reading 16 anti-detect projects. Two design rules stated as conclusions rather than options. First: 'a good fingerprint is not random and not static - it is per-site deterministic and internally coherent', per Brave's farbling model of a (session_token x eTLD+1) seed, so the same site sees the same value all session (no intra-session flicker), different sites see different values (no cross-site linking), and a new session gets fresh values. Their explicit criticism of the field: 'CloakBrowser/ChromiumFish/adryfish use one seed for all sites -> cross-site linkable ... nobody in the stealth niche has copied Brave.' Second, on input: 'Humanize = engine-level input (ChromiumFish) > client-side (CloakBrowser)', with CloakBrowser's two presets (default / careful) as the config shape to ship. Also a detection-surface matrix marking WebGPU, font list AND Skia/HarfBuzz metrics, media-device enumeration, speech voices, device sensors, and performance.now() quantization as commonly-missed surfaces.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: Two direct hits. (1) cuttle uses ONE global seed per browser - every site a seed visits sees the same canvas/audio/WebGL values, so cuttle profiles are cross-site linkable by construction; that is a deliberate tradeoff (it buys stable identity under a sticky proxy exit, per the seedIndex comment in internal/fingerprint/args.go) but it should be a WRITTEN tradeoff, not an unexamined default. (2) 'engine-level input beats client-side' is a verdict on exactly what internal/serve/humanize.go does - it rewrites CDP Input.* from outside the engine, at ~0.5s per click and ~130ms per character. Since cuttle already maintains its own patch series, the same behaviour implemented as a patch in the browser process would be both faster and unobservable from the CDP stream a driver can see. Also note the two-preset idea (default/careful): cuttle's humanization is currently all-or-nothing, and the user's pain #2/#3 (typing and secrets feel slow and fumbly) is partly a missing 'fast' preset for fields where realism does not matter.

items.what: Negative finding, stated so it is not re-searched: across all 13 issues and 7 PRs there is not one thread about file downloads, file uploads or the file chooser, screenshots, native JS dialogs (alert/confirm/beforeunload), cookie banners or overlays, popups/new tabs/target handling, secret injection or credential typing, viewport sizing for a remote viewer, VNC/remote viewing, or an LLM agent misbehaving with the tool. The one input-adjacent mention is a single sentence in #16 about a browser dying after pointer input. The repo's community is composed of fingerprint auditors filing engine-level detection bugs (@ingepanch13011, @fetchhh) and persona-coverage requesters (@aizen218); clearcote positions itself as a drop-in Playwright BINARY and pushes all driver ergonomics to Playwright itself, so the agent-experience surface simply never comes up.
items.why_it_matters_to_cuttle: Sets expectations for further mining: cuttle's four stated agent-experience pains (window does not fill the viewer, secrets/typing fumbling, downloads and screenshots being a hassle, blindness to native dialogs) have no prior art in this repo and will not be found by digging further here - those answers live in the driver-layer projects (playwright, agent-browser, browser-use, patchright/rebrowser-patches) rather than in an engine fork. What this repo IS worth re-checking periodically is the stealth-regression catalogue and the free-build release cadence, since several confirmed fixes (canvas uniform-fill, WebGL2 extension list, TURN/UDP leak, the unoptimised binary) are shipped only in their paid 151 line and the public 149 build still carries the defects - the maintainer repeatedly says a free build is 'roughly 1.5 months' out, i.e. around late September 2026.
